title: For the legal profession
primary_topics: PBA-speech doctrinal column March 30, 2014 -- first installment of three-part WTO-globalization arc (A420 → A419 Apr 6 → forward)
Philippine Bar Association (oldest and most prestigious voluntary lawyers' group; Beda Fajardo president) March 26 speech context; full speech at cjpanganiban.com self-citation
Three-part messages summary: (1) competent and ethical lawyers (2) safeguard liberty and nurture prosperity (3) help globalize the legal profession

First message: competent + ethical + responsible + dependable + morally upright + courageously uphold truth and justice; shyster-lawyers defending the indefensible via delay tactics (witnesses forget/tire/die, judges retire/promoted, victims give up); prosecution-lawyers skewing cases via bribery + defective informations + evidence-omission + frequent-absences
Filing baseless charges, whether for money or malice, 'not only unethical, also brazenly criminal'

Second message: safeguard liberty + nurture prosperity (signature FLP framing); American constitutional inheritance from French Revolution + English Magna Carta; Patrick Henry 'Give me liberty or give me death' coinage; Filipino resistance against Spanish + American + bad-governance

Filipino-First 1987 economic context vs post-WTO globalization shift: government basic-industry failure example -- National Power Corp. lost almost a trillion pesos, rotating blackouts early 1990s; WTO January 1, 1995 dawn

Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997) -- CJP's unanimously-concurred ponencia upholding WTO Treaty; verbatim ruling quote: 'Constitution mandates bias in favor of Filipino goods/services/labor/enterprises... recognizes need for business exchange... on bases of equality and reciprocity... limits protection... only against foreign competition... unfair... did not intend to pursue an isolationist policy'
Global-village framing + national-interest pragmatism; Russia + China joined WTO; only hermit-state North Korea has not entered WTO; 'to prosper, we must learn to compete globally'

Third message: globalize legal profession -- Filipino lawyers practicing abroad to help 10M OFWs and Philippine enterprises operating globally; Philippine conglomerates' overseas expansion enumerated (San Miguel + PAL + SM Investments + Robinsons Land + Metrobank + LT Group + Liwayway/Oishi-China + Ayala-Vietnam/Burma + Petron-Malaysia + Meralco-Singapore/Nigeria + Metro Pacific-Indonesia/Thailand + EDC-Chile/Ecuador + Jollibee/Cebu Pacific/ICTSI-all-over); Rule 138 amendment proposal (admit foreign lawyers for foreign law, not Philippine law, with reciprocity)
sub_topics: Philippine Bar Association, oldest and most prestigious voluntary lawyers' group headed by Beda Fajardo, met last March 26
As guest speaker, CJP had three messages, summarized as follows (full speech at cjpanganiban.com)
First, CJP looks for competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable and morally upright
And who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else
These simple values will keep our people's faith in our profession and in the rule of law
Some shyster-lawyers defend the indefensible by delaying cases
In hope that witnesses would forget the facts, or get tired, or die
Or that presiding judges would retire or get promoted, thereby passing cases to new magistrates who had no opportunity to observe witnesses on the stand
Or that victims would give up the fight
On the other hand, prosecution lawyers at times skew cases by blatant bribery and by subtler methods
Like filing of defective information (charge sheets), omission of vital evidence and frequent absences during trials
While accused may find solace in their eventual acquittal, they still have to undergo humiliation at being arrested
And to incur expenses, anxiety, and loss of time
Filing baseless charges, whether for money or malice, is not only unethical -- it is also brazenly criminal
Second, let us safeguard liberty and nurture prosperity
We inherited our constitutional framework from Americans who enshrined liberating cries of French Revolution and English Magna Carta in their Constitution
Their revolutionary ideals are captured in Patrick Henry's hypnotic oration, 'Give me liberty or give me death'
So it is with our people
We fought Spanish and American colonization, and our own leaders' bad governance
That is why our basic laws guarantee the political aspirations of our people
In singing hosannas to protect human rights, our courts liberally copy American jurisprudence
How CJP wishes the same vigor and vitality to uphold our political rights would also be used to promote our economic rights
Our 1987 Constitution was promulgated when prevailing economic mantra was 'Filipino First'
Our laws restricted entry of foreign goods and services, promoted Filipino enterprises and products even if at times they were inferior in quality and price
At that time, government operated basic industries
Result was a disaster -- not only was government grossly inefficient, it also lost heavily
National Power Corp. alone lost almost a trillion pesos and yet failed to produce enough electricity
Resulting in rotating blackouts in early 1990s
Soon after our new Constitution was ratified in 1987, world changed and abandoned protectionist economic theories
Liberalization, globalization, deregulation and privatization bloomed when WTO was born on Jan. 1, 1995
Philippine adherence to WTO was challenged in Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997)
On ground that WTO Treaty allegedly violated economic nationalism
This novel case was assigned to CJP in 1995 when he joined the SC
In upholding WTO Treaty, CJP's unanimously-concurred ponencia argued:
'While Constitution mandates a bias in favor of Filipino goods, services, labor and enterprises'
'It recognizes the need for business exchange with the rest of the world on the bases of equality and reciprocity'
'And limits protection of Filipino enterprises only against foreign competition and trade practices that are unfair'
'In other words, Constitution did not intend to pursue an isolationist policy'
'It did not shut out foreign investments, goods and services in the development of the Philippine economy'
May CJP stress that in embracing globalization, our country pursued its national interest
We recognized stark reality that world has become a global village where no country can progress in isolation
Even socialist countries like Russia and China joined the WTO
Only hermit states like North Korea have not entered the WTO
To prosper, we must learn to compete globally
Third, let us help globalize legal profession so Filipino lawyers can practice in foreign countries
To help our 10 million overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) and assist Philippine enterprises operate in foreign markets
Our OFWs brought in over $26 billion last year
San Miguel Corp. and Philippine Airlines have long been world-class brands
But after globalization dawned in 1990s, more Philippine companies expanded overseas
Like SM Investments, Robinsons Land, Metrobank, LT Group and Liwayway Marketing (makers of Oishi) in China
Ayala in Vietnam and Burma (Myanmar)
Petron in Malaysia
Meralco in Singapore and Nigeria
Metro Pacific in Indonesia and Thailand
Energy Development Corp. in Chile and Ecuador
Jollibee, Cebu Pacific Air and ICTSI, all over the world
These conglomerates need Filipino lawyers to practice in these foreign lands
To ensure that their businesses conform to our laws
In same manner that multinationals operating here want their foreign lawyers to check whether their operations here conform to laws of their countries
However, Rule 138 of Rules of Court limits admission to bar to Filipino citizens
CJP believes this should be amended to allow foreign lawyers to practice here, not about Philippine law but about foreign law
Provided Filipino lawyers are given reciprocal privileges to practice in their home states

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of a three-part WTO-globalization arc, anchored on his PBA March 26 speech. The Philippine Bar Association, the oldest and most prestigious voluntary lawyers' group headed by Beda Fajardo, met last March 26 -- as guest speaker, CJ had three messages, summarized as follows (full speech at cjpanganiban.com). First, CJ looks for competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable and morally upright, and who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else -- these simple values will keep our people's faith in our profession and in the rule of law. Some shyster-lawyers defend the indefensible by delaying cases in the hope that witnesses would forget the facts, get tired, or die; or that presiding judges would retire or get promoted, passing cases to new magistrates who had no opportunity to observe the witnesses on the stand; or that the victims would give up the fight. On the other hand, prosecution lawyers at times skew cases by blatant bribery and by subtler methods, like the filing of defective information (charge sheets), omission of vital evidence and frequent absences during trials. While the accused may find solace in their eventual acquittal, they still have to undergo humiliation at being arrested, and to incur expenses, anxiety, and loss of time. Filing baseless charges, whether for money or malice, is not only unethical -- it is also brazenly criminal. Second, let us safeguard liberty and nurture prosperity. We inherited our constitutional framework from the Americans who enshrined the liberating cries of the French Revolution and the English Magna Carta in their Constitution. Their revolutionary ideals are captured in Patrick Henry's hypnotic oration, 'Give me liberty or give me death.' So it is with our people: we fought Spanish and American colonization, and our own leaders' bad governance; that is why our basic laws guarantee the political aspirations of our people. In singing hosannas to protect human rights, our courts liberally copy American jurisprudence -- how CJ wishes the same vigor and vitality to uphold our political rights would also be used to promote our economic rights. Our 1987 Constitution was promulgated when the prevailing economic mantra was 'Filipino First' -- our laws restricted the entry of foreign goods and services and promoted Filipino enterprises and products even if at times they were inferior in quality and price; at that time, the government operated basic industries; the result was a disaster -- not only was the government grossly inefficient, it also lost heavily: the National Power Corp. alone lost almost a trillion pesos and yet failed to produce enough electricity, resulting in rotating blackouts in the early 1990s. Soon after our new Constitution was ratified in 1987, the world changed and abandoned protectionist economic theories -- liberalization, globalization, deregulation and privatization bloomed when the WTO was born on Jan 1, 1995. The Philippine adherence to the WTO was challenged in Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997), on the ground that the WTO Treaty allegedly violated economic nationalism; this novel case was assigned to CJ in 1995 when he joined the SC. In upholding the WTO Treaty, CJ's unanimously-concurred ponencia argued: 'While the Constitution mandates a bias in favor of Filipino goods, services, labor and enterprises, it recognizes the need for business exchange with the rest of the world on the bases of equality and reciprocity, and limits protection of Filipino enterprises only against foreign competition and trade practices that are unfair; in other words, the Constitution did not intend to pursue an isolationist policy; it did not shut out foreign investments, goods and services in the development of the Philippine economy.' May CJ stress that in embracing globalization, our country pursued its national interest -- we recognized the stark reality that the world has become a global village where no country can progress in isolation; even socialist countries like Russia and China joined the WTO; only hermit states like North Korea have not entered the WTO; to prosper, we must learn to compete globally. Third, let us help globalize the legal profession so Filipino lawyers can practice in foreign countries to help our 10 million OFWs and assist Philippine enterprises operate in foreign markets -- our OFWs brought in over $26 billion last year. San Miguel Corp. and Philippine Airlines have long been world-class brands; but after globalization dawned in the 1990s, more Philippine companies expanded overseas, like SM Investments, Robinsons Land, Metrobank, LT Group and Liwayway Marketing (makers of Oishi) in China; Ayala in Vietnam and Burma (Myanmar); Petron in Malaysia; Meralco in Singapore and Nigeria; Metro Pacific in Indonesia and Thailand; Energy Development Corp. in Chile and Ecuador; and Jollibee, Cebu Pacific Air and ICTSI, all over the world. These conglomerates need Filipino lawyers to practice in these foreign lands to ensure that their businesses conform to our laws, in the same manner that multinationals operating here want their foreign lawyers to check whether their operations here conform to the laws of their countries. However, Rule 138 of the Rules of Court limits admission to the bar to Filipino citizens -- CJ believes this should be amended to allow foreign lawyers to practice here, not about Philippine law but about foreign law, provided Filipino lawyers are given reciprocal privileges to practice in their home states.
